description: We are a team who like to study the metheorological changes in the Earth's surface.
summary:
Solaris is an interactive platform where users can visualize the changes of the Earth's surface. By transforming complex satellite observations into accessible visual information, Solaris aims to connect scientific data with real-world situations and the development of education.
The platform's main distinctive characteristic is that it presents the visualizations like if they were the portraits of a museum, so in that way the user can appreciate and understand the 'why' beneath each picture.
Solaris is a key tool in understanding how our planet surface's changes is essential for environmental monitoring, agriculture, risk awareness, and informed decision-making. We believe that making Earth observation data more accessible can help bridge the gap between advanced space technology and the people who can benefit from it.
details:
Solaris is an initiative to make the satelital information provided by NASA accesible and comprehensible for every kind of public, wether is people driven by their curisoity or the ones that are looking for rigorous information that can be easily visualized. We aimed for a dinamic aproach where everything is in a videogame like 3D space and also can be used for educational purposes in a practical way. Everything is made to acomplish the main objetive to make science more ingrained in the society facilitating the acces to complex but useful information that can help to solve from small problems in communities all around the world to create awareness about geodetic, fluvial and other phenomena that occurs in the geosphere, for example.

What it does. Solaris opens as a small 3D museum where every painting is a tool: (1) Global Explorer: real NISAR radar swaths from NASA GIBS on a globe, and 21 places with measured interferograms you can step through pass by pass; (2) Is my neighbourhood sinking?: search a place on a 3D city map and read the line-of-sight motion the radar measured, with its uncertainty; (3) Floods: compare surface water between two dates with NASA's OPERA product and get the area that changed in km²; (4) Date comparison and report views; (5) Terrain on your table: a 3D model of any measured place, viewable in augmented reality with one QR code (iOS and Android); (6) a 7-step introduction and practice minigames that teach how to read radar.

How it works. A Python pipeline reads NISAR L2 GUNW and GCOV products from the Alaska Satellite Facility, applies a coherence mask, removes a planar ramp, applies the ionospheric correction when present, and stores per-pixel uncertainty. The web app is plain JavaScript with three.js and MapLibre GL, served as a static site; a small serverless function queries NASA CMR and Harmony for points outside the pre-processed places.

Honesty by design. Displacement is shown along the radar line of sight (positive = toward the satellite), without atmospheric correction, and the app says so. Each value carries its 1-sigma uncertainty and is compared with a 3-sigma detection limit. Where there is no measurement, the app says there is none. Nothing is simulated except the practice minigames, which are labelled as such.

Limits. The time series covers about three months. The any-address query depends on NASA's Harmony service answering in time; inside the 21 measured places the values are always available. Augmented reality on real surfaces needs a phone with ARCore or an iPhone.

Tools. JavaScript, three.js, MapLibre GL JS, Vite, Python (h5py, numpy), IBM Carbon design tokens and icons, IBM Plex fonts, Vercel.
